blogs.title: Zoo Bite, No Anti-Biotics: *Capnocytophaga* and the Rise of CM-HUS
blogs.description: Explore the emerging link between *Capnocytophaga canimorsus* infections and Thrombotic Microangiopathy. Learn why missed prophylactic antibiotics in dog bite victims can lead to fulminant sepsis, measuring the clinical risk that these bacterial triggers can mimic 'hyperinfection' states and lead to rare complications like complement-mediated HUS. We review the presentation of 'septic shock' that quickly devolves into TMA.

blogs.title: ADAMTS13 on the Line: Distinguishing TTP from Atypical HUS in Sepsis
blogs.description: Critical teaching point on differential diagnosis for TMA. This post outlines how to triage patients with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury during sepsis. It emphasizes the utility of ADAMTS13 activity levels (specifically >10% ruling out TTP) and the pitfalls of assuming sepsis-DIC is the sole cause when schistocytes and renal failure appear.

blogs.title: Twisted Complement Pathways: Why C3 and C4 are Normal
blogs.description: A detailed look at the interpretive challenges of complement testing in CM-HUS. Clinicians are often confused by normal C3 and C4 levels in patients with complement-mediated disease. We discuss why these serological markers may remain within reference ranges despite alternative pathway activation and how functional assays or genetic testing remains essential when standard labs are inconclusive.

blogs.title: When to Block the Complement: Risks of Eculizumab in Active Infection
blogs.description: Management dilemma: Does starting eculizumab in the presence of active bacteraemia create a risk of fulminant sepsis or meningococcemia? We analyze the balance between the immediate need to halt complement activation versus the necessity of terminal proteins for bacterial lysis. This case study's decision to delay inhibitors until cultures were negative is examined.

blogs.title: The Delayed Hemolysis Trap: Identifying Complement-Mediated TMA After Sepsis
blogs.description: Clinical pearls on the evolution of TMA following infection. In many cases, TMA/myopathic syndrome does not present synchronously with the primary infection but may manifest during the 'winding down' phase of sepatis recovery. We highlight signs like isolated hemolysis rising in platelets despite improving sepsis markers and why not all hemolysis is autoimmune.
